items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Structures that have the same basic anatomy because they were inherited from a common ancestor, though they may have different functions"?
items.answer: homologous structures
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of homologous structures.

items.stem: "Selective breeding creates new genes in the animals being bred." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Selective breeding selects among existing heritable variation (alleles); new alleles only arise by mutation.
items.markingKey: Selective breeding selects among existing heritable variation (alleles); new alleles only arise by mutation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why are similarities in base sequences strong evidence for common ancestry?
options: Sequences are acquired from the environment.
Sequences are identical in all species.
Sequences are copied with small changes from generation to generation, so shared sequences are inherited from a common ancestor.
All species need the same sequences to survive.
items.answer: Sequences are copied with small changes from generation to generation, so shared sequences are inherited from a common ancestor.
items.markingKey: C. Neutral or non-coding similarities are hard to explain any other way.

items.stem: Using the domestication of dogs from grey wolves as an example, explain selective breeding as evidence for evolution.
items.answer: Over at least 15 000 years, selection produced breeds as different as chihuahuas and Great Danes, all of the same species. Large heritable changes in a short time show how selection can change a species.
items.markingKey: Context (Over at least 15 000 years, selection produced breeds as different as chihuahuas and Great Danes, all of the same species.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large heritable changes in a short time show how selection can change a species. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to selective breeding as evidence for evolution.

items.stem: Describe how you would compare the pentadactyl limbs of a frog, a bird and a human to show homology. State the bones you would identify.
items.answer: Identify in each: one upper bone (humerus), two lower bones (radius and ulna), wrist bones (carpals), palm bones (metacarpals), digits (phalanges); note modifications: fused bones in bird wing, long digits in humans, frog radio-ulna fused.
items.markingKey: Identify in each: one upper bone (humerus), two lower bones (radius and ulna), wrist bones (carpals), palm bones (metacarpals), digits (phalanges); note modifications: fused bones in bird wing, long digits in humans, frog radio-ulna fused.

items.stem:
On Daphne Major in the Galápagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured the beak depth of medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis). A severe drought in 1977 reduced the supply of small, soft seeds; mainly large, hard seeds remained.

Year | Population | Mean beak depth / mm
1976 | 1226 | 9.11
1977 | 161 | 9.67
1978 | — | 9.61

The standard deviation of beak depth in 1976 was 1.04 mm.

(a) Calculate the percentage of the 1976 population that survived to 1977. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in mean beak depth from 1976 to 1977. [2]
(c) Explain the change in mean beak depth between 1976 and 1977. [3]
(d) Explain why the offspring produced in 1978 also had deeper beaks than the 1976 population. [2]
items.answer: (a) 13.1 % (b) +6.1 % (c) Variation in beak depth existed; during the drought only large hard seeds remained; birds with deeper beaks could crack them, survived and reproduced; so the mean beak depth of the survivors increased. (d) Beak depth is heritable; survivors passed alleles for deeper beaks to their offspring, so allele frequencies changed – evolution.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 161/1226 × 100 (M1) = 13.1 % (A1). (b) [2] (9.67 − 9.11)/9.11 × 100 (M1) = +6.1 % (A1). (c) [3] Variation present (A1); large seeds the selection pressure (A1); deeper-beaked birds survive (A1). (d) [2] Heritability (A1); allele frequency change between generations (A1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Base sequence data are more convincing evidence for evolution than homologous anatomical structures."
items.answer: Sequence data are more quantitative and can resolve relationships that anatomy cannot, but evidence is most convincing when molecular and anatomical data independently agree.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sequences provide many objective, quantifiable characters; shared non-functional sequences (pseudogenes, viral insertions) are very hard to explain without common descent. Arguments against: homologous structures were the first strong evidence and are visible in fossils; both lines of evidence agree, so each strengthens the other. Supported judgement: Sequence data are more quantitative and can resolve relationships that anatomy cannot, but evidence is most convincing when molecular and anatomical data independently agree.

items.stem: Outline three types of evidence for evolution, using a specific example for each.
items.answer: Base sequences: e.g. cytochrome c or human–chimp DNA similarity; shared pseudogenes such as GULO. Selective breeding: dogs from wolves, Brassica crops, maize from teosinte – large change in short time. Homologous structures: pentadactyl limb in bat, whale, human – common ancestry. Fossils (optional): sequence of forms in rocks.
items.markingKey: Base sequences: e.g. cytochrome c or human–chimp DNA similarity; shared pseudogenes such as GULO. Selective breeding: dogs from wolves, Brassica crops, maize from teosinte – large change in short time. Homologous structures: pentadactyl limb in bat, whale, human – common ancestry. Fossils (optional): sequence of forms in rocks.

items.stem: Define the term "vestigial structure".
items.answer: A reduced structure that had a function in an ancestor but has little or no function in the present organism
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reduced structure that had a function in an ancestor but has little or no function in the present organism. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how comparison of base sequences is used as evidence for evolution.
items.answer: Homologous genes are compared between species; the number of differences increases with the time since species diverged; patterns of similarity match those from anatomy and fossils, supporting common ancestry.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Homologous genes are compared between species; the number of differences increases with the time since species diverged; patterns of similarity match those from anatomy and fossils, supporting common ancestry. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between natural selection and selective breeding (artificial selection).
items.answer: In natural selection the environment determines which variants survive and reproduce; in selective breeding humans choose which individuals breed according to desired traits; both change allele frequencies of heritable characteristics over generations.
items.markingKey: In natural selection the environment determines which variants survive and reproduce; in selective breeding humans choose which individuals breed according to desired traits; both change allele frequencies of heritable characteristics over generations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between selective breeding (artificial selection) and natural selection.
items.answer: In natural selection the environment determines which variants survive and reproduce; in selective breeding humans choose which individuals breed according to desired traits; both change allele frequencies of heritable characteristics over generations.
items.markingKey: In natural selection the environment determines which variants survive and reproduce; in selective breeding humans choose which individuals breed according to desired traits; both change allele frequencies of heritable characteristics over generations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Two species share a broken (non-functional) copy of the GULO gene needed to make vitamin C, with the same inactivating mutation. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The mutation occurred independently twice in the same way.
Both species need vitamin C from the gene.
The mutation occurred in a common ancestor of both species.
The gene was transferred between them by viruses.
items.answer: The mutation occurred in a common ancestor of both species.
items.markingKey: C. Shared identical mutations indicate common descent (e.g. humans and other primates).

items.stem: Mean milk yield of a herd of dairy cattle increased from 2650 litres per year to 9659 litres per year over 100 generations of selective breeding. Calculate the percentage increase and the mean increase per generation. Explain why this provides evidence for evolution.
items.answer: 264 %; 70.1 litres per year per generation; heritable traits changed through selection over generations
items.markingKey: (9659 − 2650)/2650 × 100 = 264 % (A1); (9659 − 2650)/100 = 70.1 litres per year per generation (A1). Heritable variation selected over generations changes the population’s characteristics – same principle as natural selection (R1).

items.stem:
On Daphne Major in the Galápagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured the beak depth of medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis). A severe drought in 1977 reduced the supply of small, soft seeds; mainly large, hard seeds remained.

Year | Population | Mean beak depth / mm
1976 | 1370 | 9.32
1977 | 176 | 9.92
1978 | — | 9.81

The standard deviation of beak depth in 1976 was 0.95 mm.

(a) Calculate the percentage of the 1976 population that survived to 1977. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in mean beak depth from 1976 to 1977. [2]
(c) Explain the change in mean beak depth between 1976 and 1977. [3]
(d) Explain why the offspring produced in 1978 also had deeper beaks than the 1976 population. [2]
items.answer: (a) 12.8 % (b) +6.4 % (c) Variation in beak depth existed; during the drought only large hard seeds remained; birds with deeper beaks could crack them, survived and reproduced; so the mean beak depth of the survivors increased. (d) Beak depth is heritable; survivors passed alleles for deeper beaks to their offspring, so allele frequencies changed – evolution.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 176/1370 × 100 (M1) = 12.8 % (A1). (b) [2] (9.92 − 9.32)/9.32 × 100 (M1) = +6.4 % (A1). (c) [3] Variation present (A1); large seeds the selection pressure (A1); deeper-beaked birds survive (A1). (d) [2] Heritability (A1); allele frequency change between generations (A1).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "analogous structures".
items.answer: Structures with a similar function and appearance that evolved independently and do not share a common ancestral origin
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: structures with a similar function and appearance that evolved independently and do not share a common ancestral origin. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Bird wings and bat wings are homologous because they both are used for flight." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: As forelimbs they are homologous (pentadactyl limb), but as wings they are analogous: flight evolved independently, with feathers in birds and skin membranes in bats.
items.markingKey: As forelimbs they are homologous (pentadactyl limb), but as wings they are analogous: flight evolved independently, with feathers in birds and skin membranes in bats. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which statement correctly links homologous and analogous structures to types of evolution?
options: Analogous structures result from divergent evolution.
Homologous structures result from divergent evolution; analogous structures from convergent evolution.
Homologous structures result from convergent evolution.
items.answer: Homologous structures result from divergent evolution; analogous structures from convergent evolution.
items.markingKey: C. Divergence modifies a shared structure; convergence produces similar ones independently.

items.stem: Moles (Eurasia) and marsupial moles (Australia) both have reduced eyes, spade-like forelimbs and dense fur. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Similar selection pressures from burrowing produced similar adaptations independently.
items.answer: Similar selection pressures from burrowing produced similar adaptations independently.
items.markingKey: B. Classic convergence between placental and marsupial mammals.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the cacti of the Americas and the euphorbias of Africa shows analogous structures.
items.answer: Both have succulent stems, spines and reduced leaves for water storage and protection in deserts. Their similar forms evolved independently in response to arid conditions; flowers and DNA show they are unrelated.
items.markingKey: Context (Both have succulent stems, spines and reduced leaves for water storage and protection in deserts.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Their similar forms evolved independently in response to arid conditions; flowers and DNA show they are unrelated. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to analogous structures.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Convergent evolution shows that evolution is predictable."
items.answer: Convergence shows evolution is constrained and partly predictable in broad outline, but historical contingency means details cannot be predicted.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: similar environments repeatedly produce similar solutions, e.g. streamlining, eyes, succulence; experiments with Anolis lizards and Lenski’s E. coli show repeated similar adaptations. Arguments against: many lineages in similar environments evolve different solutions; chance events such as mutation and drift make the exact course of evolution unpredictable. Supported judgement: Convergence shows evolution is constrained and partly predictable in broad outline, but historical contingency means details cannot be predicted.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The independent evolution of similar features in unrelated lineages as adaptations to similar environments or ways of life"?
items.answer: convergent evolution
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of convergent evolution.

items.stem: Explain the difference between analogous structures and homologous structures.
items.answer: Homologous structures share the same basic structure because of common ancestry, though functions may differ; analogous structures have similar functions but different structures and origins, evolving by convergence.
items.markingKey: Homologous structures share the same basic structure because of common ancestry, though functions may differ; analogous structures have similar functions but different structures and origins, evolving by convergence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how convergent evolution can produce analogous structures.
items.answer: Unrelated species living in similar environments face similar selection pressures; individuals with variations that improve survival in that environment reproduce more; over many generations similar structures evolve independently in each lineage, e.g. streamlined bodies in sharks and dolphins.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Unrelated species living in similar environments face similar selection pressures; individuals with variations that improve survival in that environment reproduce more; over many generations similar structures evolve independently in each lineage, e.g. streamlined bodies in sharks and dolphins. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to the thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus) and the grey wolf (Canis lupus), explain how it illustrates convergent evolution.
items.answer: A marsupial and a placental mammal evolved very similar skull shapes and body form as large predators. Similar niches produced similar features despite the lineages having separated about 160 million years ago.
items.markingKey: Context (A marsupial and a placental mammal evolved very similar skull shapes and body form as large predators.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Similar niches produced similar features despite the lineages having separated about 160 million years ago. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to convergent evolution.

items.stem: Distinguish between convergent and divergent evolution, using examples of homologous and analogous structures.
items.answer: Divergent: common ancestor, different environments, homologous structures – pentadactyl limb in bat, whale, human. Convergent: unrelated, similar environments, analogous structures – wings of birds and insects, cacti and euphorbias, shark and dolphin shape, thylacine and wolf. Significance for classification.
items.markingKey: Divergent: common ancestor, different environments, homologous structures – pentadactyl limb in bat, whale, human. Convergent: unrelated, similar environments, analogous structures – wings of birds and insects, cacti and euphorbias, shark and dolphin shape, thylacine and wolf. Significance for classification.

items.stem: Two populations of crickets mature and breed in different seasons. This is
items.answer: temporal isolation
items.markingKey: temporal isolation. Breeding at different times prevents interbreeding.

items.stem: A student claims: "Any geographical barrier immediately creates new species." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The barrier only stops gene flow; speciation follows only after the gene pools diverge enough to cause reproductive isolation.
items.markingKey: The barrier only stops gene flow; speciation follows only after the gene pools diverge enough to cause reproductive isolation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between behavioural isolation and temporal isolation.
items.answer: Behavioural isolation results from differences in courtship or mating signals; temporal isolation results from breeding at different times of day or year.
items.markingKey: Behavioural isolation results from differences in courtship or mating signals; temporal isolation results from breeding at different times of day or year. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Two populations of a fish in one lake feed at different depths and now prefer to mate with fish of their own colour. Which type of speciation is occurring?
items.answer: sympatric speciation with behavioural isolation
items.markingKey: A. Same area; mate choice isolates gene pools (e.g. cichlids in Lake Victoria).

items.stem: Outline one way in which cichlid fish in Lake Victoria shows reproductive isolation and speciation.
items.answer: Hundreds of species evolved in about 15 000 years; females choose males by colour, and populations specialise in different food. Mate choice for colour causes behavioural isolation and rapid speciation without geographical barriers.
items.markingKey: Context (Hundreds of species evolved in about 15 000 years; females choose males by colour, and populations specialise in different food.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Mate choice for colour causes behavioural isolation and rapid speciation without geographical barriers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reproductive isolation and speciation.

items.stem: Priya writes: "Any geographical barrier immediately creates new species." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The barrier only stops gene flow; speciation follows only after the gene pools diverge enough to cause reproductive isolation.
items.markingKey: The barrier only stops gene flow; speciation follows only after the gene pools diverge enough to cause reproductive isolation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how reproductive isolation can lead to speciation, distinguishing between allopatric and sympatric speciation.
items.answer: Speciation = split; need isolation of gene pools + differential selection; allopatric – barrier (bonobos/chimps, Congo River); sympatric – behavioural (cichlids), temporal (Rhagoletis), polyploidy; eventual inability to produce fertile offspring; gradual divergence.
items.markingKey: Speciation = split; need isolation of gene pools + differential selection; allopatric – barrier (bonobos/chimps, Congo River); sympatric – behavioural (cichlids), temporal (Rhagoletis), polyploidy; eventual inability to produce fertile offspring; gradual divergence.

items.stem: "Allopatric speciation is far more common than sympatric speciation." Discuss.
items.answer: Allopatric speciation is probably most common in animals, but sympatric speciation, especially by polyploidy in plants, is significant; relative frequency differs between groups.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: geographical isolation easily stops gene flow, as in many island and river examples; most well-documented speciation events involve geographical separation. Arguments against: polyploidy is a common sympatric mechanism in plants, perhaps 15 % of plant speciation events; cichlids and apple maggot flies show sympatric speciation in animals. Supported judgement: Allopatric speciation is probably most common in animals, but sympatric speciation, especially by polyploidy in plants, is significant; relative frequency differs between groups. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Define the term "temporal isolation".
items.answer: Reproductive isolation caused by populations breeding at different times of day or year
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: reproductive isolation caused by populations breeding at different times of day or year. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why bonobos and chimpanzees are considered separate species.
items.answer: They were geographically isolated by the Congo River for 1–2 million years; their populations diverged in behaviour, morphology and genes; they do not interbreed in the wild.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They were geographically isolated by the Congo River for 1–2 million years; their populations diverged in behaviour, morphology and genes; they do not interbreed in the wild. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why does a geographical barrier lead to speciation?
options: It prevents gene flow, so populations accumulate different mutations and are selected differently.
items.answer: It prevents gene flow, so populations accumulate different mutations and are selected differently.
items.markingKey: C. Separated gene pools diverge until reproductive isolation is complete.

items.stem: With reference to bonobos (Pan paniscus) and chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes), explain how it illustrates allopatric speciation.
items.answer: Populations south of the Congo River were separated from those north of it about 1–2 million years ago. Geographical isolation stopped gene flow and the populations diverged into two species.
items.markingKey: Context (Populations south of the Congo River were separated from those north of it about 1–2 million years ago.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Geographical isolation stopped gene flow and the populations diverged into two species. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to allopatric speciation.

items.stem: Two bird populations on either side of a new mountain range differ in song after 10 000 years. When reunited they do not interbreed. What has occurred?
items.answer: allopatric speciation
items.markingKey: B. Geographical isolation led to reproductive isolation.

items.stem: Using cichlid fish in Lake Victoria as an example, explain reproductive isolation and speciation.
items.answer: Hundreds of species evolved in about 15 000 years; females choose males by colour, and populations specialise in different food. Mate choice for colour causes behavioural isolation and rapid speciation without geographical barriers.
items.markingKey: Context (Hundreds of species evolved in about 15 000 years; females choose males by colour, and populations specialise in different food.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Mate choice for colour causes behavioural isolation and rapid speciation without geographical barriers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reproductive isolation and speciation.

items.stem: "Allopatric speciation is far more common than sympatric speciation." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Allopatric speciation is probably most common in animals, but sympatric speciation, especially by polyploidy in plants, is significant; relative frequency differs between groups.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: geographical isolation easily stops gene flow, as in many island and river examples; most well-documented speciation events involve geographical separation. Arguments against: polyploidy is a common sympatric mechanism in plants, perhaps 15 % of plant speciation events; cichlids and apple maggot flies show sympatric speciation in animals. Supported judgement: Allopatric speciation is probably most common in animals, but sympatric speciation, especially by polyploidy in plants, is significant; relative frequency differs between groups. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which is a classic example of adaptive radiation?
options: Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands
items.answer: Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands
items.markingKey: D. About 15 species evolved from one ancestor, with beaks for different foods.

items.stem: Why can an allopolyploid formed by chromosome doubling be fertile when the original hybrid was sterile?
options: Each chromosome now has a homologue to pair with during meiosis.
items.answer: Each chromosome now has a homologue to pair with during meiosis.
items.markingKey: A. Restored pairing allows balanced gametes.

items.stem: "Adaptive radiation is the same as convergent evolution." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Adaptive radiation is divergence from one ancestor into many forms; convergent evolution is unrelated lineages becoming similar.
items.markingKey: Adaptive radiation is divergence from one ancestor into many forms; convergent evolution is unrelated lineages becoming similar. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Two species of Tragopogon have diploid numbers 2n = 18 and 2n = 30. They hybridise. State the number of chromosomes in each gamete of the parents and in the hybrid. The hybrid is sterile, but after a doubling of chromosome number a fertile plant appears. State its chromosome number and explain why it is fertile and is a new species.
items.answer: gametes 9 and 15; hybrid 24; allopolyploid 2n = 48; every chromosome has a homologue so meiosis is normal; cannot form fertile offspring with either parent
items.markingKey: Gametes 9 and 15 (A1); hybrid 24 (A1). 48 (A1); homologues pair in meiosis (R1); crosses with parents give sterile offspring = reproductive isolation (R1).

items.stem: Explain how polyploidy and adaptive radiation each contribute to speciation, using named examples.
items.answer: Polyploidy: non-disjunction/doubling; auto vs allo; hybrid sterile; doubling restores pairing; instant reproductive isolation; examples Persicaria, wheat, Spartina anglica. Adaptive radiation: one ancestor, many vacant niches, isolation, differential selection; Darwin’s finches, Hawaiian honeycreepers, cichlids; increases biodiversity.
items.markingKey: Polyploidy: non-disjunction/doubling; auto vs allo; hybrid sterile; doubling restores pairing; instant reproductive isolation; examples Persicaria, wheat, Spartina anglica. Adaptive radiation: one ancestor, many vacant niches, isolation, differential selection; Darwin’s finches, Hawaiian honeycreepers, cichlids; increases biodiversity.

items.stem: Define the term "autopolyploidy".
items.answer: Polyploidy in which the extra chromosome sets come from the same species, e.g. by failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: polyploidy in which the extra chromosome sets come from the same species, e.g. by failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between autopolyploidy and allopolyploidy.
items.answer: Autopolyploidy involves extra sets of chromosomes from the same species (e.g. through non-disjunction); allopolyploidy involves combining chromosome sets of two different species by hybridisation followed by doubling.
items.markingKey: Autopolyploidy involves extra sets of chromosomes from the same species (e.g. through non-disjunction); allopolyploidy involves combining chromosome sets of two different species by hybridisation followed by doubling. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Hawaiian honeycreepers have beaks ranging from short and thick to long and curved. What process is best illustrated?
options: adaptive radiation from a common ancestor
items.answer: adaptive radiation from a common ancestor
items.markingKey: C. One ancestral finch-like bird diversified into many niches.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Polyploidy is the most important mechanism of speciation in flowering plants."
items.answer: Polyploidy is a major and characteristic mechanism in plants, but not the only one; its importance varies between plant groups.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: about a third or more of flowering-plant species are polyploid and many crops arose this way; polyploidy causes instant reproductive isolation. Arguments against: many plant species arise by allopatric speciation and ecological divergence; most new polyploids fail to establish. Supported judgement: Polyploidy is a major and characteristic mechanism in plants, but not the only one; its importance varies between plant groups. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: What is the wild ancestor of maize?
items.answer: teosinte
items.markingKey: A. Domestication in Mexico about 9000 years ago transformed the cob.

items.stem: Which example illustrates speciation following geographical isolation?
options: apple maggot flies on apples and hawthorns
chimpanzees and bonobos separated by the Congo River
items.answer: chimpanzees and bonobos separated by the Congo River
items.markingKey: C. The river prevented gene flow for about 1–2 million years.

items.stem: The streamlined shape of sharks (fish) and dolphins (mammals) is an example of
items.answer: convergent evolution
items.markingKey: D. Similar selection pressures in water produced similar body forms.

items.stem: Explain how adaptive radiation leads to an increase in biodiversity.
items.answer: An ancestral species reaches an area with many vacant niches; populations become isolated and specialise for different resources; differential selection and isolation cause each to become a new species, so many species arise from one.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An ancestral species reaches an area with many vacant niches; populations become isolated and specialise for different resources; differential selection and isolation cause each to become a new species, so many species arise from one. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why does selective breeding provide evidence for evolution by natural selection?
options: It proves that acquired characteristics are inherited.
It shows mutation is not needed.
It shows humans created all species.
It shows that heritable characteristics of a species can change considerably in a relatively short time when selection acts.
items.answer: It shows that heritable characteristics of a species can change considerably in a relatively short time when selection acts.
items.markingKey: D. Large changes occur through selection of heritable variation.

items.stem: Why does speciation require differential selection as well as isolation?
options: Different selection pressures cause the gene pools to diverge in adaptive traits.
Isolation alone always produces identical species.
items.answer: Different selection pressures cause the gene pools to diverge in adaptive traits.
items.markingKey: C. Drift alone may also cause divergence but slowly.

items.stem: Explain the difference between homologous structures and analogous structures.
items.answer: Homologous structures share the same basic structure because of common ancestry, though functions may differ; analogous structures have similar functions but different structures and origins, evolving by convergence.
items.markingKey: Homologous structures share the same basic structure because of common ancestry, though functions may differ; analogous structures have similar functions but different structures and origins, evolving by convergence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: What promotes adaptive radiation on newly formed islands?
options: strong competition from many existing species
many vacant niches and isolation from the mainland
continuous gene flow from the mainland
items.answer: many vacant niches and isolation from the mainland
items.markingKey: C. Empty niches allow divergence.

items.stem: Priya writes: "Homologous structures always have the same function." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Homologous structures share structure and origin, but often have different functions, e.g. bat wing and human arm.
items.markingKey: Homologous structures share structure and origin, but often have different functions, e.g. bat wing and human arm. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

1976 | 1247 | 9.23

"Bird wings and bat wings are homologous because they both are used for flight." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: As forelimbs they are homologous (pentadactyl limb), but as wings they are analogous: flight evolved independently, with feathers in birds and skin membranes in bats.
items.markingKey: As forelimbs they are homologous (pentadactyl limb), but as wings they are analogous: flight evolved independently, with feathers in birds and skin membranes in bats. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands and explain what it reveals about adaptive radiation.
items.answer: About 15 species evolved from a single ancestral species that arrived from South America about 2 million years ago, with beaks adapted for seeds, insects, cactus and even blood. Vacant niches on isolated islands allowed one ancestor to diversify into species with different feeding adaptations.
items.markingKey: Context (About 15 species evolved from a single ancestral species that arrived from South America about 2 million years ago, with beaks adapted for seeds, insects, cactus and even blood.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Vacant niches on isolated islands allowed one ancestor to diversify into species with different feeding adaptations. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to adaptive radiation.

items.stem: Mean fleece mass of Merino sheep increased from 3.3 kg to 5.7 kg over 80 generations of selective breeding. Calculate the percentage increase and the mean increase per generation. Explain why this provides evidence for evolution.
items.answer: 73 %; 0.0300 kg per generation; heritable traits changed through selection over generations
items.markingKey: (5.7 − 3.3)/3.3 × 100 = 73 % (A1); (5.7 − 3.3)/80 = 0.0300 kg per generation (A1). Heritable variation selected over generations changes the population’s characteristics – same principle as natural selection (R1).

items.stem: Briefly describe cichlid fish in Lake Victoria and explain what it reveals about reproductive isolation and speciation.
items.answer: Hundreds of species evolved in about 15 000 years; females choose males by colour, and populations specialise in different food. Mate choice for colour causes behavioural isolation and rapid speciation without geographical barriers.
items.markingKey: Context (Hundreds of species evolved in about 15 000 years; females choose males by colour, and populations specialise in different food.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Mate choice for colour causes behavioural isolation and rapid speciation without geographical barriers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reproductive isolation and speciation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Convergent evolution means two species are becoming one species." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Convergence produces similar features in unrelated species; they remain separate lineages and cannot interbreed.
items.markingKey: Convergence produces similar features in unrelated species; they remain separate lineages and cannot interbreed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: About 15 species evolved from a single ancestral species that arrived from South America about 2 million years ago, with beaks adapted for seeds, insects, cactus and even blood. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Base sequence data are more convincing evidence for evolution than homologous anatomical structures."
items.answer: Sequence data are more quantitative and can resolve relationships that anatomy cannot, but evidence is most convincing when molecular and anatomical data independently agree.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sequences provide many objective, quantifiable characters; shared non-functional sequences (pseudogenes, viral insertions) are very hard to explain without common descent. Arguments against: homologous structures were the first strong evidence and are visible in fossils; both lines of evidence agree, so each strengthens the other. Supported judgement: Sequence data are more quantitative and can resolve relationships that anatomy cannot, but evidence is most convincing when molecular and anatomical data independently agree.

items.stem: "Allopatric speciation is far more common than sympatric speciation." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Allopatric speciation is probably most common in animals, but sympatric speciation, especially by polyploidy in plants, is significant; relative frequency differs between groups.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: geographical isolation easily stops gene flow, as in many island and river examples; most well-documented speciation events involve geographical separation. Arguments against: polyploidy is a common sympatric mechanism in plants, perhaps 15 % of plant speciation events; cichlids and apple maggot flies show sympatric speciation in animals. Supported judgement: Allopatric speciation is probably most common in animals, but sympatric speciation, especially by polyploidy in plants, is significant; relative frequency differs between groups. items.stem: "Convergent evolution shows that evolution is predictable." Discuss.
items.answer: Convergence shows evolution is constrained and partly predictable in broad outline, but historical contingency means details cannot be predicted.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: similar environments repeatedly produce similar solutions, e.g. streamlining, eyes, succulence; experiments with Anolis lizards and Lenski’s E. coli show repeated similar adaptations. Arguments against: many lineages in similar environments evolve different solutions; chance events such as mutation and drift make the exact course of evolution unpredictable. Supported judgement: Convergence shows evolution is constrained and partly predictable in broad outline, but historical contingency means details cannot be predicted. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Polyploidy is the most important mechanism of speciation in flowering plants." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Polyploidy is a major and characteristic mechanism in plants, but not the only one; its importance varies between plant groups.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: about a third or more of flowering-plant species are polyploid and many crops arose this way; polyploidy causes instant reproductive isolation. Arguments against: many plant species arise by allopatric speciation and ecological divergence; most new polyploids fail to establish. Supported judgement: Polyploidy is a major and characteristic mechanism in plants, but not the only one; its importance varies between plant groups. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "selective breeding"?
options: Speciation that occurs when populations are separated geographically
Artificial selection in which humans choose individuals with desired traits to breed, changing the characteristics of domesticated species over generations
Polyploidy in which the extra chromosome sets come from the same species, e.g. by failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis
The accumulation of differences between related populations, often leading to new species with different adaptations
items.answer: Artificial selection in which humans choose individuals with desired traits to breed, changing the characteristics of domesticated species over generations
items.markingKey: B. "selective breeding" is artificial selection in which humans choose individuals with desired traits to breed, changing the characteristics of domesticated species over generations.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "behavioural isolation"?
options: Polyploidy arising from hybridisation between two species followed by doubling of the chromosome number
The condition of having more than two complete sets of chromosomes in a cell
Reproductive isolation caused by differences in courtship or mating behaviour
A reduced structure that had a function in an ancestor but has little or no function in the present organism
items.answer: Reproductive isolation caused by differences in courtship or mating behaviour
items.markingKey: C. "behavioural isolation" is reproductive isolation caused by differences in courtship or mating behaviour.

items.stem: Which pair are analogous structures?
items.answer: the wing of a bird and the wing of an insect
items.markingKey: the wing of a bird and the wing of an insect. Bird and insect wings evolved independently.

items.stem: Distinguish between allopolyploidy and autopolyploidy.
items.answer: Autopolyploidy involves extra sets of chromosomes from the same species (e.g. through non-disjunction); allopolyploidy involves combining chromosome sets of two different species by hybridisation followed by doubling.
items.markingKey: Autopolyploidy involves extra sets of chromosomes from the same species (e.g. through non-disjunction); allopolyploidy involves combining chromosome sets of two different species by hybridisation followed by doubling. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which observation about the pentadactyl limb best supports common ancestry rather than common function?
options: All limbs are used for walking.
Limbs of unrelated animals look similar.
Limbs evolved independently in each species.
The same bone pattern occurs in limbs used for very different functions.
items.answer: The same bone pattern occurs in limbs used for very different functions.
items.markingKey: D. Divergent function with conserved structure indicates inheritance.

items.stem: Explain how allopatric speciation can occur.
items.answer: A geographical barrier divides a population; gene flow stops; mutations, genetic drift and different selection pressures cause allele frequencies to diverge; eventually the populations become so different that they cannot interbreed even if they meet again (reproductive isolation).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A geographical barrier divides a population; gene flow stops; mutations, genetic drift and different selection pressures cause allele frequencies to diverge; eventually the populations become so different that they cannot interbreed even if they meet again (reproductive isolation). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why analogous structures can lead to errors in classification.
items.answer: Analogous structures look similar but have different evolutionary origins; grouping organisms by them would place unrelated organisms together, so classification must use homologous features and molecular data.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Analogous structures look similar but have different evolutionary origins; grouping organisms by them would place unrelated organisms together, so classification must use homologous features and molecular data. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Polyploid plants are always weaker than diploid plants." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Polyploids are often larger and more vigorous (e.g. many crops such as wheat, strawberries and potatoes are polyploid).
items.markingKey: Polyploids are often larger and more vigorous (e.g. many crops such as wheat, strawberries and potatoes are polyploid). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Homologous structures always have the same function." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Homologous structures share structure and origin, but often have different functions, e.g. bat wing and human arm.

Using the cacti of the Americas and the euphorbias of Africa as an example, explain analogous structures.
items.answer: Both have succulent stems, spines and reduced leaves for water storage and protection in deserts. Their similar forms evolved independently in response to arid conditions; flowers and DNA show they are unrelated.

items.stem: Two species of Senecio have diploid numbers 2n = 20 and 2n = 18. They hybridise. State the number of chromosomes in each gamete of the parents and in the hybrid. The hybrid is sterile, but after a doubling of chromosome number a fertile plant appears. State its chromosome number and explain why it is fertile and is a new species.
items.answer: gametes 10 and 9; hybrid 19; allopolyploid 2n = 38; every chromosome has a homologue so meiosis is normal; cannot form fertile offspring with either parent
items.markingKey: Gametes 10 and 9 (A1); hybrid 19 (A1). 38 (A1); homologues pair in meiosis (R1); crosses with parents give sterile offspring = reproductive isolation (R1).

items.stem: With reference to the domestication of dogs from grey wolves, explain how it illustrates selective breeding as evidence for evolution.
items.answer: Over at least 15 000 years, selection produced breeds as different as chihuahuas and Great Danes, all of the same species. Large heritable changes in a short time show how selection can change a species.
items.markingKey: Context (Over at least 15 000 years, selection produced breeds as different as chihuahuas and Great Danes, all of the same species.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.answer: The barrier only stops gene flow; speciation follows only after the gene pools diverge enough to cause reproductive isolation.

items.stem:
On Daphne Major in the Galápagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured the beak depth of medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis). A severe drought in 1977 reduced the supply of small, soft seeds; mainly large, hard seeds remained.

Year | Population | Mean beak depth / mm
1976 | 1258 | 9.19
1977 | 162 | 9.63
1978 | — | 9.57

The standard deviation of beak depth in 1976 was 0.91 mm.

(a) Calculate the percentage of the 1976 population that survived to 1977. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in mean beak depth from 1976 to 1977. [2]
(c) Explain the change in mean beak depth between 1976 and 1977. [3]
(d) Explain why the offspring produced in 1978 also had deeper beaks than the 1976 population. [2]
(e) The change in mean beak depth was about 0.5 standard deviations. Comment on the size of this change. [1]
(f) Suggest why this study is described as evolution being observed in action. [1]
(g) State the type of selection shown by these data. [1]
items.answer: (a) 12.9 % (b) +4.8 % (c) Variation in beak depth existed; during the drought only large hard seeds remained; birds with deeper beaks could crack them, survived and reproduced; so the mean beak depth of the survivors increased. (d) Beak depth is heritable; survivors passed alleles for deeper beaks to their offspring, so allele frequencies changed – evolution. (e) Large for one generation; shows strong directional selection. (f) The change in a heritable characteristic of the population was measured over a single generation, rather than inferred from fossils. (g) directional selection
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 162/1258 × 100 (M1) = 12.9 % (A1). (b) [2] (9.63 − 9.19)/9.19 × 100 (M1) = +4.8 % (A1). (c) [3] Variation present (A1); large seeds the selection pressure (A1); deeper-beaked birds survive (A1). (d) [2] Heritability (A1); allele frequency change between generations (A1). (e) [1] Recognises a substantial shift relative to natural variation (A1). (f) [1] Measured directly across generations / short time scale (A1). (g) [1] Directional (A1).
